claim_findings.recommendation: Add a management_guidance/management_opinion claim for the 'pipeline remains quite robust ... we expect activity levels to remain healthy' statement from seg-0003 (and/or the seg-0008 restatement), so the sustainability question has evidence on both sides in claims.json.

The problem is coverage: the run also archived evidence/web/web-001.md (a pre_event, 2026-07-09 AlphaStreet preview) giving a 14-analyst consensus of $5.67 EPS on $50.54bn revenue, with an EPS range of $5.09 to $6.56. claim_findings.recommendation: Extract a second consensus claim from web-001 so the brief can present a range or at least acknowledge vendor disagreement.

outlook_findings.passage: a materially different growth profile from Wells Fargo, whose EPS of $2.00 [claim-027] was far more pedestrian, consistent with its narrower capital-markets footprint
outlook_findings.evidence: Two compounding defects in the sentence that carries section 4's whole argument. (1) The cited claim does not support it: claim-027 contains only Wells Fargo's absolute net income ($6.4bn) and EPS ($2.00). It contains no growth rate at all, so it cannot establish a 'growth profile'. The comparison being drawn is between EPS levels across different companies (Goldman's $20.98 in claim-026 versus Wells Fargo's $2.00), which differ mainly because of share count and say nothing about performance. (2) The run's own archived source contradicts the conclusion: evidence/web/web-003.md, the document claim-027 comes from, states that Wells Fargo's diluted EPS was 'up 25% from a year ago', revenue up 9%, ROTCE up from 15.2% to 17.7%, Corporate and Investment Banking revenue up 16% and Markets revenue up 24%. Wells Fargo therefore both grew strongly and participated in the capital-markets strength. The brief's only piece of discriminating counterevidence for its central 'sector-wide cycle, not company-specific alpha' thesis is thus unsupported by the claim it cites and contradicted by the source sitting in this run's evidence pack.
outlook_findings.recommendation: Remove the Wells Fargo EPS-level comparison. Either drop the Wells Fargo contrast entirely and rest the sector-wide argument on the growth figures that do exist (claim-026 ROE, claim-028 net income growth, claim-029 IB fee growth), or extract a claim for Wells Fargo's actual year-on-year growth from web-003 and re-argue the point against those numbers, which currently cut the other way.

outlook_findings.passage: deploys more of its targeted $40 billion of excess capital at its stated 17% return goal [claim-018][claim-019], then fee income and capital deployment reinforce each other without introducing new pricing or volume risk. The consequence is that ROTCE holds near or above this quarter's 23% [claim-001]
outlook_findings.evidence: The upside case's mechanism does not follow from its own cited claims and is arithmetically backwards. claim-019 puts the deployment target return at 17%; claim-001 puts current ROTCE at 23%. Deploying incremental capital at a 17% return dilutes a 23% ROTCE rather than holding it 'near or above' it. Separately, 'without introducing new pricing or volume risk' is asserted with no supporting claim and runs against the transcript the claims come from, where Jamie Dimon says of deployment 'we do think we'll deploy it, and that has consequences' (seg-0079). This is an upside case whose conditions-to-consequence chain breaks in the middle.
outlook_findings.recommendation: Rewrite the upside case so the consequence follows from the cited claims: either drop the capital-deployment leg and rest the ROTCE case on sustained fee income, or state plainly that deployment at a 17% target return would be accretive to earnings but dilutive to a 23% ROTCE. Remove the unsupported 'without introducing new pricing or volume risk' clause.

outlook_findings.passage: comfortably ahead of the $5.52 Wall Street consensus set ahead of the print [claim-001][claim-024][claim-025]
outlook_findings.evidence: The brief presents $5.52 as 'the' Wall Street consensus, and section 9 says only that no full-year consensus was captured. Neither passage tells the reader that this run archived a second pre-print consensus (evidence/web/web-001.md, dated 2026-07-09, temporal_status pre_event) putting the 14-analyst consensus at $5.67 EPS on $50.54bn revenue, with EPS estimates spanning $5.09 to $6.56. The revenue estimates differ by $1.8bn between the two vendors. The beat conclusion survives either number, so the direction is not wrong, but 'comfortably ahead of the consensus' overstates the precision of a single-vendor figure when the run holds a conflicting one. Section 2 repeats the same framing ('the pre-print consensus of $5.52'), dropping even the Zacks attribution that claim-024 carries.
outlook_findings.recommendation: Attribute the number ('the Zacks consensus of $5.52') and note in section 9 that another archived pre-print source in this run gives a 14-analyst consensus of $5.67 with a $5.09-$6.56 range, so the size of the beat is vendor-dependent.

The statements are true against the transcript, but they are attributed to a claim that does not contain them, so a reader auditing the brief through claims.json cannot verify them.
outlook_findings.recommendation: Either extract a claim for the seg-0074 answer and cite it alongside claim-021, or cut the lending-demand and attribution-caution language and let the sentence carry only what claim-021 actually says.

outlook_findings.passage: is the better read on the "core franchise" trend, and it is decelerating relative to the CIB/Markets pace
outlook_findings.evidence: 'Decelerating' asserts a change in CCB's own growth rate over time. No cited claim establishes that: claim-007 gives a single year-on-year growth rate of 8% for one quarter, and the run contains no prior-period CCB growth rate to compare it with. What the evidence supports is only that CCB grew more slowly than CIB in this quarter, which is a level difference, not a trend.
outlook_findings.recommendation: Replace 'decelerating relative to the CIB/Markets pace' with a level statement, e.g. 'growing well below the CIB/Markets pace', unless a prior-period CCB growth claim is added.

summary: One high-severity finding blocks this run. Section 4's Wells Fargo contrast - the only discriminating counterevidence for the brief's central thesis that this was a sector-wide capital-markets cycle rather than JPMorgan-specific execution - compares EPS levels across different companies ($20.98 versus $2.00), is not supported by the claim it cites (claim-027 carries no growth rate), and is contradicted by the very document that claim comes from: web-003 shows Wells Fargo EPS up 25% year-on-year with Markets revenue up 24% and CIB revenue up 16%. Three medium findings follow: the upside case's ROTCE mechanism is backwards (deploying capital at a 17% target return dilutes a 23% ROTCE rather than holding it), the $5.52 consensus is presented as definitive while the run archived a conflicting $5.67 fourteen-analyst consensus, and an AI-CapEx sentence attributes lending-demand commentary to claim-021, which does not contain it. On the claims side, the extractor captured management's cautionary comments on Investment Banking sustainability but not its explicit 'pipeline remains quite robust ... we expect activity levels to remain healthy' statement from the same passage, leaving the evidence pack one-sided on the question the brief turns on. Sourcing, provenance, period labelling and temporal integrity are otherwise sound: the archived peer documents are genuine, the one undated source the brief relies on is verifiably pre-print, quarter-versus-half-year period labels are correct throughout, the injection scan is clean, and the prose is industry-appropriate for a bank.
